newsitem.title: UK: UK pension funds warn Labour on two-tier tax.
newsitem.headline: UK pension funds warn Labour on two-tier tax.

text.p: Britain's National Association of Pension Funds warned the opposition Labour party that the introduction of a two-tier capital gains tax would reduce stock market liquidity and undermine the City of London.

Labour has said it is considering a two-tier tax system, under which investors would pay less tax if they hold assets over a longer period, in an effort to combat what it regards as a damagingly short-term investment culture in Britain.

Graham Allen, chairman of the NAPF Investment Committee who also manages Imperical Chemical Industries' pension fund, told a fringe meeting at the Labour party conference that a two-tier tax could be damaging and that investment institutions could simply resort to derivatives to avoid it.
"It would certainly result in reduced liquidity in the market and would make London less attractive. It would be detrimental to the City of London," he said.

Labour's shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, Alistair Darling, told the same meeting that the party had not come to any conclusion yet on whether to establish a two-tier capital gains tax. "But there are arguments to be looked at," he said.
Labour was aware that if a tax regime was too complex, it encouraged evasion, Darling added.

Allen challenged suggestions that pension funds, which control around a third of all shares listed on the London Stock Exchange, were among the main offenders as far as short-termism was concerned, arguing that they tended to hold shares for very long periods.
"They aim to create a portfolio whose value will rise. They will adopt a buy-and-hold strategy in the main," he said. "I would firmly contend that pension funds are very patient investors."
While acknowledging that some British companies paid dividends which were too high, Allen disputed charges that this was because of pressure from large institutional investors for short-term returns.
"Why should pension funds prefer these cash payments when their objective is the long-term health of the companies in which they invest?" he asked.
"I do not believe fund managers can intimidate financial directors and chief executives in this way."

There were numerous examples of pension funds having supported cuts in dividends. It was often the case that companies had little idea how to invest their profits and chose to pay higher dividends instead.

"Company managers are not blameless. Some believe it would be wimpish to cut dividends and would send the wrong signals," undermining their share price and leaving them vulnerable to takeovers, Allen said.
He said institutions were beginning to take a more active role in monitoring companies in which they had shares. "I think we will see more intervention but not necessarily in public."
Darling said the culture of short-termism was not limited to instutional investors. "Lousy management" had also been a problem while politicians were one of the groups most guilty of short-termism.

"I question whether short-termism can be dealt with by any legislative change," Darling said, but the threat of legislation could have a salutary effect in encouraging a change of behaviour. He urged institutions to take a closer interest in companies in which they hold stakes and to act more like owners.
